Microchipped humans

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What is the future of humans being microchipped to perform every day functions, normally done with external devices?

Summary:
The first microchip was implanted into a human in the UK in 1998. Since then there have been a few advances in the technology, but it has not become a mainstream practice. In South Africa there are two engineers who are working on ways to use implanted intelligent microchips in everyday life and to solve some of South Africa's issues with access to good health care.
Daniel De Kock and Jarryd Becker have implanted microchips into their skin. These microchips are the size of grains of rice and have the potential to start cars using program codes, send signals of biographical information (barcodes) to computers and phones within close proximity and also posses the power to provide geographical location information of the host. It is expected that in the future, the chips will have medical uses such as monitoring blood sugar or sounding an alarm if a heart attack is imminent. South African Law enables tests for the implanted chips – which are not allowed the same way under US regulation.

Professor Basie Von Solms is a professor at UJ and a specialists in cyber security, he can give us a broader perspective on how these intelligent microchips are being used internationally and what the security risks are if this becomes more common practice.

That is the basic overview. It is insane though when you listen to them talk about using implants to go beyond correcting a medical fault in the human body to actually turning humans into wireless super humans. To make us able to pay for things, start our cars, gain security access and provide our medical history by swiping our hand or arm near the device.

Further information:
What we would be able to see
The egineers programming an implant. An implant being put into one of the engineers hands the same implant then being used to open a security gate.
A Dutch traveler has become the first person to travel without a physical boarding pass. The passenger had a microchip implanted in his hand that had all relevant travel documents. An experiment using an NFC microchip allowed the traveler to breeze through airport security without ever needing to hand over a his boarding pass for identification. Instead, the traveler scanned his hand on an NFC chip reader and was passed through security with the swipe of his wrist
There is a Youtube video available to use in the show
There are are also being used to create ‘digital tatoos’. One of the guys has implanted a microchip that if scanned by a phone becomes a video art piece. So they also be used to store data, which can be read by an external device.
Other information about the current Global use of these implants:
1. Martijn Wismeijer, Dutch creator of a bitcoin ATM, has placed an RFID in his hand to store his Bitcoin private key.

2. In 2002 Verichip verimed – was a company in the states that opened providing implants with medical records, but hospitals and rescue workers had to have the scanner in order to read the implant. But they closed down after being sued for faking how many hospitals actully agreed to carry the scanner.
3. A Swedish company has implanted microchips in its employees' hands Chips allow staff to use the photocopier and even pay for their lunch

4. Another suggested application for a tracking implant, discussed in 2008 by the legislature of Indonesia's Irian Jaya would be to monitor the activities of persons infected with HIV, aimed at reducing their chances of infecting other people.[19][20] The microchipping section was not, however, included into the final version of the provincial HIV/AIDS Handling bylaw passed by the legislature in December 2008

5. Theoretically, a GPS-enabled chip could one day make it possible for individuals to be physically located by latitude, longitude, altitude, speed, and direction of movement.

6. Since nearly all implantable microchips are unencrypted, they are extremely vulnerable to being read by third-party scanners. By scanning secretly, someone could steal the information on a chip and clone the signal, enabling that person to impersonate a chipped individual.

Press Release:


Microchipped Humans
Could implanting an intelligent microchip the size of a grain of rice into your body change the way you start a car, send information to a computer or phone, or even help in a medical emergency? Carte Blanche meets the young South African engineers who implanted these devices beneath their skin ‘for fun’ and to test the potential for this technology to change everyday life.


Script:


Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
00:00 Entrance to DIZ Innovation Zone.
Music.
Interview with Darryn De Kock and Jarryd Bakker Darryn: We both studied the same discipline we both did megatronic engineering

Jarryd: We spent half our time in corporate RND. So Darryn: we do projects that the other engineers find kind of scary, because they are cross-disciplinary.

Jarryd: We are called bushveld Labs.

Darryn: We started out in the middle of Pretoria somewhere in the bushveld so we just assumed the name and then moved to Braamfontein and then the name stuck and then our company kind of an implantable technology.
00:31 - 00:55 Bongani link to microchip Bongani: 40 years ago if you’ve been told that you would be walking around with smart mobile phones well the idea would’ve seemed laughable but today they are everywhere and similarly if we talk about humans being implanted with intelligent microchip in the future the reaction is “ That’s crazy right?” well don’t laugh to hard.
00:55 – 01:13 Bongani sitting with Darryn and Jarryd demonstrating the chip Bongani: Jarryd Bekker and Darryn De Cock crudely started implanting these intelligent microchip under their skin almost three years ago. They are the only south Africans in this tech research and use themselves as case studies.
01:13 -01:30 V/O: Toby Shapshak is the publisher of the Technology and Innovation Publication stuff magazine.

Toby: People are fascinated by how to get technology into their bodies to make their lives easier. They put very basic RFID chips or more complex MFC chips into their bodies.
01:30 – 03:02 Darryn: RFID which is a classic what you put in a pet we have adopted NFC now because most of the smart phones have that. Inside each chip they are very much the same you have a little antenna around a core and then that antenna goes into an energy harvesting unit which can receive RFID power and turn that into a little energy for the chip to use and that powers the little transponder in the chip in the back and that allows it to speak out to the rest of the world. So it can send receive and store information.

Bongani: how is it going to add to our everyday life in a practical way?

Darryn: so I think a nice example would my trip from home to work and back everyday. So leaving my home as I walk out the house it arms my house then I put my hand out to my door handle and it open the door and it just opens, I get into my car, I drive to the gautrain station and walk through the boom I put my hand on the gautrain reader and it lets me through, I get to work and I scan at the door and it knows that I’m there. I get in a do some work, lunch time comes I pop down to the shops and pick out the stuff that I want to east for lunch I get to the pay terminal I put my chip against it the payment processed. Imagine then if you had this implant and it was capturing a lot of aspects of your life that goes to some aspect of the AI and that AI can process that abstract data. If I meet someone in a club and I kind of like them and I want to see if are we compatible we can literally bump our chips and we can get a sense of how compatible we are in the same way that fermions would indicate compatibility we could digitally mimic those pheromones.

03:02 – 03:21 Bongani: have you tried to approach corporate and see if they have some use for them in their wider public at large?

Darryn: yeah there is two that we are interested in now and we have tried to initiate talks but there is a lot of red tape to get through and I think as people start to understand that red tape people start to fall away.
03:21 – 03:30 V/O: Professor Basie von Solms is the director for the centre for cyber security and electro academy for computer science and software engineering at the University of Johannesburg
03:30 – 04:02 Bongani: so this will boil down to the right of the individual vs. that of society at large?

Professor: Every chip that you implant in your body has got a privacy consequence finding out whom you are? Checking your position through GPS that’s a privacy issue do I want to do that? I do it with my smart phone if I want to but I can switch it off. Everything we are doing here and talking about here has got a privacy consequence and I think that may be one of the reasons why are still a long way of seeing this rolled out on a much bigger scale.
04:02 – 04:11 V/O V/O: Nnamdi Oranye is the author of Africa’s first book- Disrupting Africa. That details the lives of innovators and entrepreneurs changing the African landscape.
04:11 – 04:53 Nnamdi: In South Africa and the rest of Africa we have a need space to approach technology and the need to solve immediate problems. In the first world most of these problems don’t exist which opens them up to invest and investigating forward thinking technology.

Toby: Right now its for the hobbies its for the people who try the use cases are just aren’t there yet. Generally it’s a very niche very controversial filed and it hasn’t really taken off yet in South Africa as it has international.

Nnamdi: I think with time once we figure out these needs based technology will have the capacity to focus on forward thinking technology, bio technology without a doubt will become extreme.
04:53 -05:49 Darryn speaking about body modification Darryn:” when you want to buy one right now there are a few roots, you can start right at the bottom and speak to your vet and see if you could buy a pet tag, then you can move on to a more advance NSC implant that you can get from Canada. The chips that you get online are blank then you can program them with a little link with a smartphone app to launch things to do very rudimentary tasks. If you go little bit further you can you have underground grinders they are called grinders they will go and modify their own body and implant little things. There are some guys in the states I think for a week they cut up their side and put a little Bluetooth module and another guy had it on his hard it was a big bulgy electronic device sticking out of this skin kind of of how do you do this? These guys are they are not doctors they look online, YouTube video and they learn how to operate on themselves, body modification artist.
05:49 – 06:17 V/O Bongani Bongani: everyone who is experimenting with this technology is experimenting on themselves. A Swedish engineer implanted a microchip into his hand and convinced a local airline to allow him to use the implant to go through security. Imagine a world where we no longer need boarding passes or even passports. But what are the security risks to using this technology under our skin?
06:17 – 07:06 Toby: the security risks lets say of having a id chip is that somebody else could get the same chip and same information and use to impersonate you I mean you see it in a movie like Mission Impossible all the time.

Professor: I got no doubt about it that technology could come to a point where you can implant the chip for whatever reason and with or without the agreement of the patient that you could actually control them. If somebody could hack into my chip, which it can, do remember that if that guy could come up and buy the internet to my chip now we can change the programme.

Bongani: are there laws in place in South Africa or internationally to deal with this?

Professor: in South Africa’s are not aware of any illegal environment. I don’t think under the present constitution we will ever get into a position where it can be compulsory.
07:06 -07:15 Toby: I just think that the fear of the security, the fear of invading our bodies is going to keep it at arms length
07:15 - People on streets and Bongani interviewing Darryn Bongani: so what are some of the future benefits we will see from these microchips?

Darryn: I want to upgrade myself as I get older I want to get senses and I want to make myself physically better and be more aware
